τινὲς μὲν οὖν οὕτως ἀνέγνωσαν ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐντολὴ πρώτη ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ, ὡς τῶν πρὸ
αὐτῆς ἐντολῶν οὐ περιεχουσῶν ἐπαγγελίαν· ἐπὶ γὰρ ταύτης οἴονται πρώτην
ἐπαγγελίαν κεῖσθαι τὴν ἵνα εὖ οι γένηται καὶ ἵνα μακρο χρόνιο γένῃ ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ ἧ
Κύριο ὁ Θεό ου δίδω ί οι. ἐοίκασιν δὲ οὗτοι μὴ τετηρηκέναι ἐπαγγελίαν κειμένην
καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς δευτέρας ἐντολῆς, οὐ ποιή ει γάρ, φησί, εαυτῷ εἴδωλον οὐδὲ παντὸ
ὁμοίωμα, ὅ α ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἄνω καὶ ὅ α ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω καὶ ὅ α ἐν τοῖ ὕδα ιν
ὑποκάτω τῆ γῆ · οὐ προ κυνή ει αὐτοῖ οὐδ' οὐ μὴ λατρεύ ῃ αὐτοῖ . ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι
Κύριο ὁ Θεό ου, Θεὸ ζηλωτή , ἀποδιδοὺ ἁμαρτία πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα ἕω τρίτη καὶ
τετάρτη γενεᾶ τοῖ μι οῦ ί με, καὶ ποιῶν ἔλεο εἰ χιλιάδα τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ί με καὶ τοῖ
φυλά ου ι τὰ προ τάγματά μου· παρατήρει γὰρ ὅτι ἐπαγγελία ἐστὶ τὸ ποιῶν ἔλεο εἰ
χιλιάδα τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ί με καὶ τοῖ φυλά ου ι τὰ προ τάγματά μου. μήποτ' οὖν, ἐπεὶ ἡ
∆εκάλογος πρώτη τῷ λαῷ νομοθεσία μετὰ τὸ ἐξελθεῖν τὴν Αἴγυπτον εἴρηται, ἑκάστη
τῶν δέκα ἐντολῶν πρώτη ἐστὶν ἐν πρώτοις τῶν ἑξῆς εἰρημένη. ὁ μέντοιγε θέλων
ἐπιμένειν τῇ ἀποδόσει τοῦ ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐντολὴ πρώτη ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ ἐρεῖ ὅτι ἰδία μέν
ἐστι τῆς τίμα τὸν πατέρα ου καὶ τὴν μητέρα ου ἐντολῆς ἡ ἐπαγγελία ἡ ἵνα
μακροχρόνιο γένῃ ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ ἧ Κύριο ὁ Θεό ου δίδω ί οι, οὐκ ἰδία δὲ τῆς οὐ
ποιή ει εαυτῷ εἴδωλον οὐδὲ παντὸ ὁμοίωμα ἡ ποιῶν ἔλεο εἰ χιλιάδα τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ί
με καὶ τοῖ φυλά ου ι τὰ προ τάγματά μου. πάλιν δὲ αὖ καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ἐνστήσεται ὁ
τὴν ∆εκάλογον ὅλην περιέχειν πρώτας ἐντολὰς διηγούμενος· ἐρεῖ γὰρ τὸ
μακροχρόνιον γενέσθαι ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ ἧ Κύριο ὁ Θεὸ δίδω ι τοῖς ἁγίοις οὐ διὰ μόνην
δίδοσθαι τὴν τίμα τὸν πατέρα ου καὶ τὴν μητέρα ου ἐντολὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ δι' ἄλλας
μυρίας· δεήσει τε τὸν τοιοῦτον συναγαγεῖν ἐντολὰς αἷς ἐπιφέρεται τὸ ἵνα
μακροχρόνιο γένῃ ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ , ἧ Κύριο ὁ Θεό ου δίδω ί οι. μετὰ ταῦτα ζητητέον
περὶ τῆς χαριζομένης ἐπαγγελίας τὸ μακροχρόνιον ἐπὶ τῆ γῆ ἧ Κύριο ὁ Θεὸ δίδω ι
τοῖς ἁγίοις. καὶ οὐκ ἀγνοητέον γε ὅτι κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν ἡγοῦνται τοῦτο γίνεσθαι οἱ
Ἰουδαῖοι· ἀλλ' ὁρῶμεν οὐ πάντως τοῦτο ἀληθές, φησὶ δὲ καὶ ὁ προφήτης οἴμοι ὅτι ἡ
παροικία μου ἐμακρύνθη. ζητητέον οὖν τὴν ἀγαθὴν γῆν ἣν Κύριο ὁ Θεὸ ἐν
ἐπαγγελίᾳ δίδω ι τῷ καταλιπόντι τὴν πνευματικὴν Αἴγυπτον καὶ μετὰ πάσης
μακροθυμίας καὶ ὑπομονῆς ὁδεύσαντι τὴν πνευματικὴν ἔρημον τὴν πολλὴν καὶ
φοβεράν, καὶ νικήσαντι οὓς πατά ει Κύριος βα ιλεῖ μεγάλου καὶ οὓς ἀνεῖλεν Κύριος
βα ιλεῖ κραταιού . 32 Eph. vi9 καὶ οἱ κύριοι, τὰ αὐτὰ ποιεῖτε πρὸς αὐτούς. [Ὠριγένης
δέ φησιν] τίνα τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν προειρημένων; οἶμαι οὖν ὅτι ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας καὶ τὸ
ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὸ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ μετ' εὐνοίας τῆς πρὸς τοὺς
οἰκέτας. [vi 10] τοῦ λοιποῦ ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν Κυρίῳ καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος
αὐτοῦ. τὸ δυναμοῦσθαι ἐν Κυρίῳ δυναμοῦσθαί ἐστιν ἐν λόγῳ καὶ ἐν σοφίᾳ καὶ τῇ τῆς
ἀληθείας θεωρίᾳ καὶ πάσαις ταῖς Χριστοῦ ἐπινοίαις· οὗ μέγιστόν ἐστι τὸ τῆς ἰσχύος
κράτος καὶ κραταιότερον ἀρετῆς καὶ τῶν εἰδῶν αὐτῆς, ἅτινα πάντα εἰσὶ δυνάμεις,
ὥσπερ αἱ κακίαι ἀδυναμία. ἔστι δέ τις τῶν ἀρετῶν (ὥς φασιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοί)
ἀθεώρητος ἡ καλουμένη ἰσχύς, ὠνομασμένη οὕτως τῷ ἀναλογίαν τινὰ ἔχειν πρὸς
τὴν σωματικὴν ἰσχύν, καὶ ἄλλη θεωρητός, κάλλος ἀπὸ τοῦ σωματικοῦ ὠνομασμένη,
καθ' ὃ κάλλος λέγεται, περιζῶ αι τὴν ῥομφαίαν ου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν ου, δυνατέ, τῇ
ὡραιότητί ου καὶ τῷ κάλλει ου· καὶ ἐν τῷ Ἄσματι τῶν ᾀσμάτων πρὸς τὴν νύμφην
ὅλη καλὴ εἶ πλη ίον μου, καὶ μῶμο οὐκ ἐ τὶν ἐν οί· καὶ πάλιν ἐν τεσσαρα κοστῷ
τετάρτῳ ψαλμῷ καὶ ἐπιθυμή ει ὁ βα ιλεὺ τοῦ κάλλου ου. 33 Eph. vi11 [ἐνδύσασθε
τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς στῆναι πρὸς τὰς μεθοδείας τοῦ
διαβόλου.] [Ὠριγένης δέ φησιν] ἐκ τῶν ἑξῆς καὶ τῶν περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος
pass_a_gloss: Some then read thus 'which is the first commandment in promise', as though the commandments before it do not contain a promise; for on this one they think the first promise to lie, namely 'that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you'. These seem not to have observed a promise lying also on the second commandment; for, it says, 'you shall not make for yourself an idol nor a likeness of anything, whatever is in heaven above and whatever is on the earth below and whatever is in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not bow down to them nor serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, rendering the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation to those who hate me, and doing mercy to thousands to those who love me and keep my ordinances.' For observe that 'doing mercy to thousands to those who love me and keep my ordinances' is a promise. Perhaps then, since the Decalogue was spoken as the first legislation to the people after going out of Egypt, each of the ten commandments is first, spoken among the first of those that follow. However, the one wishing to persist in the explanation of 'which is the first commandment in promise' will say that the promise 'that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you' is proper to the commandment 'honor your father and your mother', but 'doing mercy to thousands to those who love me and keep my ordinances' is not proper to 'you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness'. And again, against this too the one explaining the whole Decalogue as containing first commandments will object; for he will say that becoming long-lived upon the land which the Lord God gives to the saints is given not through the commandment 'honor your father and your mother' alone, but also through countless others; and such a one will need to gather the commandments upon which 'that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you' follows. After these things one must inquire about the promise granting long life upon the land which the Lord God gives the saints. And one must not be ignorant that the Jews consider this to happen according to the letter; but we see this is not at all true, and the prophet also says 'woe is me that my sojourning was lengthened'. One must seek then the good land which the Lord God gives in promise to the one who has left the spiritual Egypt and with all long-suffering and endurance has journeyed the spiritual desert, the great and fearful one, and has conquered those great kings whom the Lord strikes and those mighty kings whom the Lord destroyed. Eph 6:9: 'and the masters, do the same things to them.' [Origen says:] which are 'the same things' of those said before? I think then that: 'in simplicity of heart', and 'doing the will of God', and 'from the soul' and 'with goodwill' toward the household slaves. [6:10] 'For the rest, be empowered in the Lord and in the might of his strength.' To be empowered in the Lord is to be empowered in Word and in wisdom and in the contemplation of the truth and in all the conceptions (aspects) of Christ; of which the greatest is the might of strength, and mightier than virtue and its species, which all are powers, as the vices are powerlessness. And there is one of the virtues (as those clever about these things say) non-theoretical, the so-called strength, named so by having some analogy to bodily strength, and another theoretical, beauty, named from the bodily, according to which beauty it is said 'gird your sword upon your thigh, mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty'; and in the Song of Songs to the bride 'you are wholly beautiful, my near one, and there is no blemish in you'; and again in the forty-fourth psalm 'and the king will desire your beauty'. Eph 6:11 ['put on the full armor of God so that you can stand against the methods of the devil.'] [Origen says:] from the things following and from the things about the Savior (continues: written...)
pass_b_english: Some have read "which is the first commandment with a promise" (Ephesians 6:2) as if the commandments before it held no promise. For they think the first promise is set down on this one: "that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you."

But these readers seem not to have noticed that a promise lies on the second commandment as well. "You shall not make for yourself an idol," it says, "nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" (Exodus 20:4-6). Observe that "showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" is a promise.

Perhaps, then, since the Ten Commandments were given to the people as their first legislation after they came out of Egypt, each of the ten commandments is a first commandment, spoken among the first of all that followed.

Yet someone who wants to hold to the plain sense of "which is the first commandment with a promise" will say this: the promise "that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you" belongs properly to the commandment "Honor your father and your mother"; but "showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" does not belong properly to "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness."

Then again, the one who explains the whole Decalogue as made up of first commandments will object to this too. He will say that long life on the land which the Lord God gives to the saints is not given for the one commandment "Honor your father and your mother" alone, but for countless others as well. And such a person will need to gather the commandments to which "that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you" is attached.

After this we must inquire about the promise that grants long life on the land which the Lord God gives to the saints. We should not fail to see that the Jews think this comes about according to the letter. But we see that this is by no means true; the prophet too says, "Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged" (Psalm 120:5). So we must look for the good land which the Lord God gives by promise to the one who has left the spiritual Egypt, who has traveled with all patience and endurance through the spiritual wilderness, great and terrible, and who has conquered the great kings whom the Lord strikes down and the mighty kings whom the Lord has slain.

"And you masters, do the same things to them" (Ephesians 6:9). Origen says: Which of the things said before are "the same things"? I think, then, that they are "in simplicity of heart," "doing the will of God," "from the soul," and "with goodwill" toward the household servants.

"Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the might of his strength" (Ephesians 6:10). To be made strong in the Lord is to be made strong in the Word, in wisdom, in the contemplation of the truth, and in all the aspects of Christ. Of these the greatest is the might of his strength, mightier than virtue and its kinds, all of which are powers, just as the vices are powerlessness. Among the virtues, as those skilled in these matters say, there is one that is not a matter of theory, called strength, so named because it bears some likeness to bodily strength; and another that is a matter of theory, called beauty, named from bodily beauty. It is with this beauty in view that we read, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty" (Psalm 45:3); and in the Song of Songs, to the bride, "You are all beautiful, my companion, and there is no blemish in you" (Song of Solomon 4:7); and again in Psalm 45, "And the king will desire your beauty" (Psalm 45:11).

not a matter of theory (Stoic class of virtues) / a matter of theory

choices.english: not a matter of theory ... a matter of theory
choices.why: Stoic school language for virtues that are not sciences of theorems; 'unobservable/observable' (old English) misreads it.
